history.period: 1373-1375 CE (inscription dated 770 AH / 1369 CE cited by some scholars)
history.summary: NOT A HINDU TEMPLE - 14th-century Islamic mosque; keep-or-drop decision needed. Built by Sultan Sikandar Shah (r. 1358-1389), second ruler of the Ilyas Shahi dynasty, after his victories over the Delhi Sultanate, as an imperial statement of the new kingdom. Located at Pandua (then a Sultanate capital), it was the largest mosque of the Indian subcontinent in its time, with 260 stone pillars and 387 domed bays, a great vaulted central nave (now collapsed) and an enclosed courtyard modelled on the Great Mosque of Damascus. Its terracotta ornament fuses Persianate and local Pala-Sena motifs (lotus, kirtimukha on the stone minbar); carved stone from pre-Islamic structures was reused in doors, arches and facings. Inscriptions style Sikandar Shah 'the exalted Sultan' and 'Caliph of the faithful'; legend says Raja Ganesha later used it as a royal court. The Sultan was buried in a tomb chamber on the western wall. Damaged by 19th-century earthquakes and disused since; now an ASI Monument of National Importance. CSV town 'Malda' corrected to Pandua (Malda is the district / ~16-18 km-distant town).

name: Adina Mosque
town_description: Pandua (Hazrat Pandua) is a historic village in Malda district, about 18 km north of Malda town. It was a capital of the Bengal Sultanate in the 14th-15th centuries and holds ASI-protected monuments including the Adina Mosque and the Eklakhi Mausoleum.

travel.airport: Bagdogra International Airport (IXB), roughly 230 km north, is the nearest major airport.
travel.railway: Malda Town Junction (MLDT), a major station, is about 16-18 km south.
travel.road: About 16-18 km north of Malda town on Pandua Road; buses run from Rathbari More to Golghor bus stand near the site.

visitor_information.opening_hours: ASI monument; typically open sunrise to sunset with free entry (verify).
